speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To help me understand your sudden vertigo, can you describe exactly what the sensation feels like—is it a spinning of the room or just lightheadedness? Also, does moving your head in a specific way, such as rolling over in bed or looking up, trigger or worsen the symptoms?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: That sounds consistent with Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), given the brief duration and trigger. Do you experience any hearing loss, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), or a feeling of fullness in your ears?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you. Since your symptoms occurred as you were going to bed, did the vertigo start specifically when you lay down or turned your head? Also, have you had any recent head trauma or upper respiratory infections?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you have any other neurological symptoms, such as weakness, numbness, slurred speech, or double vision? Also, do you have a history of migraines or high blood pressure?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

speaker: Doctor
text:
You have denied neurological deficits and hearing issues, which is reassuring. To confirm the diagnosis, I need to perform a physical exam; please lie back with your head hanging slightly off the edge of the bed and turn your head 45 degrees to the right while I observe your eyes for nystagmus.

REQUEST TEST: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the left side, combined with the brief duration of symptoms and lack of other neurological signs, confirms the diagnosis. DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
